en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Questions of Mañjuśrī Concerning the Transformations of Sudarśana, Spoken by the Buddha.
Translated at the Mi-lin Monastery in the kingdom of Jalandhara, Central India, by the Tripiṭaka Master Ming... [name].
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Tianxi Cai, by Imperial Decree. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great multitude of bodhisattvas, including Mañjuśrī.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the youth Mañjuśrī, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!

For the sake of all sentient beings who have developed inverted views regarding the Four Noble Truths and thus constantly dwell in saṃsāra without being able to escape it, I now proclaim this Dharma of the true Four Noble Truths."
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha!
By what causes and conditions do all sentient beings fail to distance themselves from such false saṃsāra, remaining neither awakened to nor aware of it?"
The Buddha said, “Mañjuśrī!
I see sentient beings undergoing such false saṃsāra. Why is this?”
"Good son! It is all because from time immemorial one has falsely given rise to conceptual attachments and discriminated between self and other. Mañjuśrī!"
For these reasons, they undergo this retribution for their deluded karma and wander in vain through saṃsāra. Why is this?

Because these deluded sentient beings have neither heard nor known the supreme Dharma of universal quiescence; they do not reflect upon or awaken their three karmas, but instead indulge their body, speech, and mind in creating a multitude of afflictions—such as "I am greedy," "I am angry," and "I am deluded."

Now, within the Dharma of that Tathāgata, I have attained this renunciation, received the pure precepts, and practiced the pure conduct; thus I have distanced myself from saṃsāra, attained the path to nirvāṇa, and been liberated from the wheel of suffering.

Furthermore, he reflects to himself: "The nature of these afflictions is itself wholesome dharma; it is itself tainted dharma; it is itself untainted dharma; it is itself the dharma of saṃsāra; it is itself the mundane and the supramundane; it is itself wisdom and the dharma of elimination; it is itself the definitive dharma; it is itself the perfect wisdom of contemplation; it is itself the contemplation of the definitive path regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the way; and it extends even to the definitive dharma-realm."

Furthermore, he reflected: "Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are illusory, because all conditioned phenomena are suffering, and because all conditioned phenomena are signless (*animitta*), if I attain this, I shall be able to remain far removed from all that is illusory and achieve birth at will."
If one contemplates the view of self as not being separate from the Truth of the Path, one immediately attains those dharmas, and whatever one does will accord with one's intention.

Furthermore, regarding those dharmas, one maintains mindfulness without confusion; regarding all dharmas, the mind is without differentiation. One who can know in this way will be able to distance themselves from lack of faith, doubt, and slander. Praising this attainment, they shall be liberated from all suffering of the self.
At that time, there was not the slightest thing for me to find difficult to accomplish.

If an Arhat can know this "self," then at the moment of death, seeing for themselves where they shall be reborn, they cast aside their former mind, attain the Bodhi of a Buddha, and proceed with sovereign ease according to their own wishes; thus they immediately reach the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*). Therefore, they obtain this knowledge of suffering and knowledge of phenomena (*duḥkha-jñāna* and *dharma-jñāna*).
If one understands that I have compiled all these teachings, yet gives rise to a lack of faith, harbors doubt and suspicion, slanders them, or experiences various forms of fear;
if one does not believe in these teachings because they exhaust this compilation, such a person will think in this way and resolve upon the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
He further reflects: "This dharma should be practiced in this way, for by doing so one attains the truth of cessation.
If this dharma is practiced, this cessation will certainly occur; such is the certainty."
With such thoughts, doubt arose in his mind, and after his life ended, he fell into the great hells.
What is meant by "contemplating according to reality"?
It is that which gives rise to all phenomena.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how does one perceive the mind of the Four Noble Truths?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
“If one sees that all dharmas are fundamentally non-arising, this is seeing the Truth of Suffering;
if one sees that the arising of all dharmas is extinguished, this is the Truth of Origination.”
If one perceives the supreme nirvana, the dharma-characteristic of universal quiescence, this is the truth of cessation;
if one perceives the ultimate nature of all phenomena, this is the truth of the path.

Mañjuśrī! If one perceives these Four Noble Truths as neither real nor unreal, as wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas, as with-outflows or without-outflows, as mundane or supramundane, as conditioned knowledge or unconditioned knowledge, as unchanging dharmas, and as the dharmas of the discerning knowledge that contemplates suffering and its origin—then this is the definitive truth of cessation, up to and including the definitive dharma-realm of the truth of the path, which cannot be altered.
For what reason do all deluded sentient beings, being attached to sensual pleasures, become confused regarding this Dharma of the true nature?
Those sentient beings do not reflect with discernment upon the dharma of cessation; consequently, the quiescent intrinsic nature of all phenomena does not manifest before them.

One does not know this Dharma as something to be grasped, nor as something to be abandoned, nor as something apart from grasping and abandoning; for within the realm of desire, it manifests as nirvāṇa, and because it can manifest that tranquil realm of nirvāṇa within the realms of hatred, delusion, and even the realm of saṃsāra.
If one can manifest such equality of intrinsic nature within all phenomena, one shall attain unimpeded mastery over all phenomena; how then could one not know that true reality?

If, regarding phenomena that are neither born nor extinguished, the mind is like space—because the equality of the Buddha is unattainable, the equality of the Dharma is unattainable, the equality of the Saṃgha is unattainable, and even the equality of the tranquility of Nirvāṇa is unattainable.
Thus, regarding all unprecedented phenomena (*adbhuta-dharma*), one does not give rise to doubt or confusion, thereby attaining freedom from uncertainty.
This is because one reaches the realm of the most supreme nirvana, which is unborn and unarisen, and is utterly tranquil.
Mañjuśrī! Thus, because all dharmas of ultimate truth are invisible, Subhūti did not go to pay homage at the feet of the Tathāgata.
If even Subhūti has attained non-self, how much more so the Tathāgata—
how could he be seen? Do not hold such a view, Mañjuśrī!
"Because one perceives something within all these dharmas that are non-arising, this is not seeing the Four Noble Truths.
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How does one see the four foundations of mindfulness? The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"That Subhūti shall attain the contemplation of the impurity of the body and thus see the foundation of mindfulness of the body."
Contemplating that feeling is suffering is the application of mindfulness to feelings;
contemplating that the mind is impermanent is the application of mindfulness to the mind;
contemplating that phenomena are non-self is the application of mindfulness to phenomena.
Mañjuśrī again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should this true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) be explained?”
"Furthermore, how does one perceive the true four foundations of mindfulness?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Cease, for this true reality as taught by the Tathāgata is difficult to understand and difficult to know."
Mañjuśrī said: “I only pray that you will explain and extensively analyze those four foundations of mindfulness in their true nature. The Buddha said: “Mañjuśrī!
If you perceive a body equal to space, you then perceive the application of mindfulness to the body within this very body.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if one perceives anything to be attained— whether internally, externally, or in between— within sensation, one then perceives the application of mindfulness to sensation.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If one perceives this mind as having squareness or roundness, or as being large or small, one is thereby perceiving the station of mindfulness regarding the mind within the mind.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If one perceives anything to be attained within the categories of wholesome and unwholesome, outflowing and non-outflowing, or even among mundane and supramundane phenomena including those associated with afflictions, then this is not the application of mindfulness to phenomena regarding these phenomena.
"Mañjuśrī! These four foundations of mindfulness of reality should be understood in this way.
Mañjuśrī addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“What is the vision of the four right efforts?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

“If one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as ultimately empty and quiescent, even to the point of being without intrinsic nature, and perceives that all phenomena are unattainable therein, one should arouse a mind of diligence; for by conforming to the Dharma, one eliminates all unwholesome karma that has arisen.”
In order that unwholesome states not yet arisen may not arise;
in order that wholesome states not yet arisen may be brought forth by arousing a mind of diligence;
and in order that wholesome states already arisen may endure for a long time and not be forgotten—one should arouse a mind of perfect diligence.

Just as all phenomena are free from grasping, free from relinquishing, and yet not apart from grasping and relinquishing—if one attains such right mindfulness, the mind will no longer arise, and one immediately attains this practice of samādhi.
How does he contemplate? Because he has attained the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
How does he abide in the equality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-samatā*)?
“Mañjuśrī, one should view the four right efforts in this way. Mañjuśrī then spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
How are the five faculties to be viewed?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! If one perceives that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen, one then understands and gains faith in the faculty of faith. Why is this?
Mañjuśrī! This ultimate non-arising is the faculty of faith, because within all phenomena the mind cannot be apprehended; it is fundamentally free from this name.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
If, regarding all phenomena, one is free from recollection and thus has no pursuit or seeking, and does not abide in any location, this is the faculty of diligence.

Mañjuśrī! If, regarding all phenomena, one is free from manifest clarity and thus remains detached from differentiation, such that the mind does not arise, this is the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya).
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

If, regarding all phenomena, one is able to transcend arising and ceasing, and is able to realize both the subject that perceives and the object perceived, because their nature is both empty and non-empty, this constitutes the faculty of concentration.
Mañjuśrī! If, by nature, existence and non-existence are both unattainable within all phenomena, this is the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya). Mañjuśrī!
"One should understand it in this way, by thoroughly comprehending the five faculties. Mañjuśrī said,
"World-Honored One!"
"How does one perceive the five powers? The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī!
If one can perceive these vast mental phenomena as being devoid of intrinsic nature and devoid of characteristics, this is the power of faith.
Mañjuśrī! If, in seeking the merit of awakening, one is able to transcend both grasping and rejecting—and yet is not separate from grasping and rejecting—this is the power of diligence.
Mañjuśrī! If one is free from all recollections regarding all phenomena and possesses no conceptual clinging, this is the power of mindfulness. Mañjuśrī!
If one reaches the state where all phenomena are signless, this is the power of concentration. Mañjuśrī!
If one can remain far removed from all that is perceived, even up to nirvāṇa, this is the power of wisdom.
"Mañjuśrī! You should understand it in this way, for you have thoroughly realized the five powers. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
How does one perceive the seven factors of enlightenment?
The Buddha said:
“Mañjuśrī! If one perceives all phenomena as being without intrinsic nature and does not engage in recollective thought toward them, this is the factor of awakening of mindfulness. Mañjuśrī!”

If, regarding all phenomena, the mind cannot be measured or fathomed, yet one speaks of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the attainment of the prediction of enlightenment—this is the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Mañjuśrī!

If, regarding all phenomena, one is able to be free from grasping and rejecting, yet not free from grasping and rejecting, and furthermore abandons all conceptual deliberation regarding phenomena, this is the factor of enlightenment of diligence (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*).
Mañjuśrī! If one does not give rise to attachment toward any phenomena, because one understands that all phenomena are unborn, this is the factor of awakening of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Mañjuśrī! If, regarding all phenomena, one gives rise to faith and delight because one understands that all phenomena are unattainable, this is the awakening factor of pliancy.
Mañjuśrī! If, regarding all phenomena, the mind is without agitation, this is the factor of awakening of concentration. Mañjuśrī!

If one dwells in no abiding and has no attachment toward all phenomena, such that they cannot be perceived, and does not give rise to craving or clinging toward any phenomenon—if one attains this equanimity, it is called the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga).
“Mañjuśrī! The seven factors of enlightenment should be understood in this way so that they may be fully comprehended. Mañjuśrī said:
“World-Honored One!
How does one perceive the Eightfold Noble Path?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If one does not perceive correctness, nor even perceive the non-existence of all things, and sees that dharmas have no dual characteristics and the mind has no hindrances—this is right view."
Mañjuśrī! If one perceives all phenomena as being free from all obstructions, yet not non-obstructed, and the mind has no attachment, this is called right reflection.
Mañjuśrī! If one perceives all phenomena as having no limits and, in accordance with that limitlessness, explains them with equanimity and skill, this is right speech.
Mañjuśrī! If one perceives all phenomena as being without activity, free from a mind of compassion because they are fundamentally unarisen, this is right action.
Mañjuśrī! If one is without joy and without anger toward all phenomena, and no phenomena arise, this is right livelihood. Mañjuśrī!
If, regarding all phenomena, there is neither arising nor ceasing, and no functional efficacy, this is right effort (*samyag-vīrya*).
Mañjuśrī! If, regarding all phenomena, there is no arising in every thought-moment, no cognitive perception, and one is free from all conceptualization, this is right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
Mañjuśrī! If one can remain detached from all phenomena, whether regarding their intrinsic nature or the absence of such nature, and has no point of attachment, this is called right concentration.
“Mañjuśrī! This Eightfold Noble Path should be understood in this way, and thus one can fully comprehend it. “Mañjuśrī! [he said.]

If one perceives these four noble truths with the mind, one immediately attains the vision of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.

By virtue of a true mind, they seek the further shore and reach the stage of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), attaining great peace and bliss; having cast off all heavy burdens, they are far removed from dust and free from defilement, contemplating the formlessness of the body until they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Arhat, the Śramaṇa, and the Brāhmaṇa who has reached the further shore of purity is called "one of great learning. He is a true son of the Buddha, a son of the Muni;

he can overcome his enemies, cast off the afflictions, and attain great steadfastness. Being without old age, without fear, without doubt, and without conceptual proliferation, being neither "that" nor "this," such a bhikṣu is called the "Sacred Banner of the Dharma."
Mañjuśrī! If one attains such patience regarding the Dharma, one obtains great and wholesome benefit, and should receive offerings from all the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras.

Mañjuśrī! Therefore, one who ensures that no land passes by in vain will receive offerings of pure food and drink; for the sake of departing from saṃsāra and reaching the shore of nirvāṇa, and for liberation from the wheel of suffering, up to the attainment of all-knowledge and perfect enlightenment, they shall obtain whatever is sought through the arousal of this mental state.

At that time, when the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma, thirty-two thousand devaputras all attained this Dharma. Those hosts of devas scattered mandārava flowers and mahāmandārava flowers as an offering to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, and spoke these words:
"They shall go forth into homelessness within the Buddha-Dharma of the Tathāgata and receive the pure precepts."
"If one listens to and receives this Dharma with a single-minded focus, one shall attain the path to Bodhi.
Furthermore, eight thousand one hundred bhikṣus attained the liberation of the exhaustion of outflows and the realization of non-arising;
additionally, forty-two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

At that time, throughout the trichiliocosm, all the palaces of the Māra kings, the mountains, forests, wildernesses, and the great earth shook in six ways, while a rain of various celestial flowers fell from the void, as they proclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"It is most rare indeed that this Dharma has been so well expounded!
This sound resounded throughout the ten directions.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince, along with the great bodhisattvas, the assembly of bhikṣus, and all the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others in the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, each rejoiced, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew.
The Scripture on Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into the Dharma Spoken by the Buddha
